Stretching across Peru’s arid Nazca desert, some 250 miles south of Lima, the mysterious Nazca Lines have fascinated and puzzled both locals and visitors for almost two millennia. These enormous geoglyphs—some hundreds of yards long—have kept their true purpose veiled in secrecy to this day, sparking both wild theories and meticulous scientific research. Ready to unravel what experts really think is behind these giant drawings? Buckle up for a mind-bending journey into the heart of one of archaeology’s biggest enigmas.

Discovery and Rediscovery Through the Centuries

Although the people of the Nazca region have always known about these earth drawings, the first written mention dates all the way back to 1553. Pedro Cieza de León, a Spanish conquistador, referred to them in his book Crónicas del Perú, though he didn’t provide a clear description (mysterious, even by 16th-century standards).

The official rediscovery of the Nazca Lines happened in 1927, thanks to Peruvian archaeologist Toribio Mejía Xesspe, who spotted several outlines while surveying the nearby hills. In the 1940s, American anthropologist Paul Kosok and, soon after, German mathematician Maria Reiche took up the scientific baton—studying, mapping, and even actively fighting to protect the geoglyphs.

Monumental Designs in the Desert

Cut into the Peruvian desert almost 2,000 years ago, the famous Nazca Hummingbird still hasn’t given up the secret of its existence. Since 1994, these geoglyphs have been a UNESCO World Heritage site, covering an area of about 175 square miles (450 square kilometers, for our metric friends).

  • Some 800 geometric figures have been engraved onto the desert floor, each consisting of a single, unbroken line.
  • Among these, you’ll find straight lines, spirals, ellipses, trapezoids, triangles—and plenty of stylized plants and animals such as monkeys, hummingbirds, condors, jaguars, spiders, cacti, as well as human figures and some pretty odd characters no one’s quite sure how to classify.

How Were the Nazca Lines Made?

Maria Reiche estimated most of the figures were drawn over about a thousand years, between 500 BCE and 500 CE, by groups connected to the Paracas and Nazca cultures. Their method? Ingeniously simple: workers removed the darker, sun-oxidized pebbles from the surface to reveal the lighter soil underneath. The shallow grooves survived the test of time, mainly thanks to the region’s extreme aridity—Mother Nature’s own preservation technique.

Evidence suggests the Nazca artists used a technique called carroyage—basically a grid system. They’d divide a design into small squares and then scale it up on the ground using stakes and ropes. In support of this, an excavation in the 1940s uncovered 300 wooden stakes near a giant rectangle about half a mile long (800 meters) and over 300 feet wide (100 meters). The finding lent serious weight to this hypothesis.

Decoding the Mystery: From Star Maps to Sacred Paths

For decades, the leading theory was an astronomical one—some lines point towards the sun on certain dates, fueling ideas of ancient observatories. But as it turns out, there are far too many orientations and directions for a single, coherent system of star plotting.

Today, archaeologists believe the Nazca Lines most likely had a range of complementary functions:

  • The long lines and massive trapezoids may have served as ceremonial pathways for community gatherings dedicated to water and fertility.
  • Animal and plant shapes echo motifs found on Nazca pottery, suggesting the drawings transformed the desert into a sacred landscape.

As for those theories about ancient alien runways—don’t bet your tinfoil hat on them, as there’s no serious evidence to support such claims.

And the story keeps evolving. In 2024, a team from Japan’s Yamagata University, working with IBM Research, announced the discovery of 303 additional geoglyphs. With the help of AI analysis of aerial images, they found these smaller geoglyphs, often hidden near ancient trails and much harder to spot. This fresh insight suggests that the grand, linear figures likely marked routes for public rituals, while the smaller shapes may have functioned as landmarks guiding pilgrims to ceremonial sites.
